Dropped by Best Buy today and they had an in-store demo of the PlayStation VR. I don't own a PS4 but being interested in the tech (and being a gamer) I figured I'd give it a go. Previous to this I'd only tried Samsung Gear VR and Google Cardboard.

They offered 5 demo options. I can't remember the names of the games...one was a tank game and one was a space shooter (I saw another guy play the space shooter). Since I'm not familiar with the PS4 controller I opted to do a demo of an undersea "experience" where you just look around. The gear consisted of the visor and a separate (but large) set of headphones.

The first thing I noticed was the fairly significant gap at the bottom of the visor which let too much light in. I'm skeptical that this was just the lady fitting the headset incorrectly--the unit would have to be on pretty darn tight to close that gap. Of course I was sitting in BB under super-bright lights which didn't help. The next thing I noted was the pixelation (sp?) of the graphics. Don't get me wrong, it didn't look "bad" but you could definitely see pixels fairly easily. The visual fidelity wasn't as superior to the Gear VR or Google Cardboard as I'd expected. Finally, the corded nature of the headset was a bit cumbersome even whilst sitting. At one point I reached back to adjust it and the headset went black for a couple of seconds. Those "cons" aside, the rest of the demo was pretty cool. Basically the sim involved just sitting in a cage and being lowered in the ocean where you look around and finally a shark breaks your cage and lunges at you. I was pretty impressed with the fact that leaning towards something in the virtual world worked perfectly (things got closer). I also stood up out of my chair a couple of times and that worked flawlessly as well. The sim I did had very little movement (some swaying within the cage) so I didn't experience any motion sickness, but when the shark began knocking the cage around I could sense how it might make you feel queasy. The big "seller" within the demo were some jump scares toward the end when the shark penetrated the cage and lunges directly at you. That did illicit flinching despite the pixelation.

If I had a PS4 I'm not 100% sure I'd be tempted to spend $400 for this upgrade. It was neat and with the right titles I'm sure it'll be awesome--but it's clearly version 1.0. Never having tried the Vive or Rift I have no idea how it compares. I will say this--it was pretty clear from the demo that this style of gaming will take off in a major way...based on this demo, however, I'm more inclined to wait another few years for them to iron out some of the kinks.

I've tried out my friends oculus rift dev kit before and can definitely say the screen door effect caused by being so close to the display is quite noticable. The rift had no positional tracking however so standing up or leaning forward did nothing to the position of the in game camera. Still all this considered it's quite an experience. In the right setting it's easy to forget you're just sitting at a chair.

I'd love to get a hold of an HTC vive and try it out, it looks like the best VR experience out there but it's expensive as hell. Curious as to how the display is in that one though. I am definitely convinced as well that vr will take off pretty well. It really does change the entire way you see the game. Even if you're just sitting still with no motion controls.

"Screen door effect" is the phrase I should have used. Although that didn't necessarily detract from my experience, I'm sure in another few years we'd look back at issues like that and cringe...hence me not being enthusiastic about forking out a wad of cash for the first generation. The positional tracking of the PlayStation VR was very good, however. It tracked perfectly and the visual fidelity improved--e.g. I leaned to my right to look at some gauges and the closer I got I could read them better.

One thing I'm almost 100% sure of--this type gear will profoundly impact game design as well as game genres. The technology IS compelling, but it will obviously work best in certain types of games. For example, there's a novelty to standing up and walking around with the stuff on, but that's not practical in an FPS like Doom where you're jumping and climbing at high rates of speed. Flying and driving sims, however, lend themselves perfectly to this gear. Obviously devs will adapt, but games written with this type of gear in mind will probably be substantially different in their design in order to conform to the limits of the hardware.

I bought an HTC Vive. The Vive is $800 vs $400, so it's a more premium model. The Vive does not have the gap you mentioned. There is a tiny hold at the bottom that you can see out of but it's out of your sight line unless you deliberately point your eyes directly downward.

The cord at the back is annoying on the Vive too, but the headset doesn't blink out when you fiddle with it. The head tracking and controller tracking are phenomenal. I was stunned at how well the tracking is. In game you actually see the handsets and their movements are perfect. If you put the two controllers directly touching each other they are tracked and perfectly touch in game.

The resolution is amazing, the headset is comfortable, and the entire experience is immersive. The only drawback of the Vive is the price tag and the fact that you need a top of the line PC to run it (which I guess is just double down on "price tag"). $800 for the unit + $1600 for a PC that can run it is pretty steep.

This experience sounds a lot like what you'd get from the rift DK2. It's not terrible, but it's far from perfect. The effect you're describing is often refereed to as "the screen door effect" and it has to do with the pixel density not being high enough for a screen that sits so close to your face. You do get used to it after a while, but you're definitely going to notice it the first time you put the headset on.

The biggest drawback to this is that it makes smaller text illegible. This is a bit of a problem for games where you might occasionally have to read something. Elite: Dangerous is a title that definitely has this problem with the DK2. On the upside, because it's a Sony device made for a Sony system the software will likely be designed using larger fonts so it's a non-issue. I'm rather surprised that they pulled it off at all considering the limitations of the PS4.
